lead: The helm turns the rudder and the rudder turns the boat, but only while water flows past it. Steer with small movements and say what you are about to do, and the crew can trust the deck under their feet.

sections.title: Which way to move the helm

qa.q: Which way do I push the tiller to turn the bow to port?
qa.a: To starboard: a **tiller** works the opposite way to a wheel, so you move it away from where you want the bow to go. A wheel steers like a car.

blocks.p: A **wheel** steers like a car: turn it clockwise, to starboard, and the bow goes to starboard. A **tiller** works the other way: push it to starboard and the bow swings to port. Move a tiller away from where you want the bow to go.

To **bear away** is to turn the bow away from the wind; to **luff up** is to turn it towards the wind. Sitting on the windward side with a tiller, you pull it towards you to bear away and push it away from you to luff up.

fig.note: Tiller to windward: the bow bears away

blocks.p: **Head to wind** means the bow points straight into the wind, as when the mainsail is hoisted under engine. You are there when the wind arrow at the masthead points dead ahead.

qa.q: The compass shows 130° but I should steer 140°. Which way do I turn?
qa.a: To starboard: compass headings grow **clockwise**, so you turn to starboard until it reads 140°. To bring the number down, you turn to port.

blocks.p: Compass headings grow **clockwise**. If the skipper gives you 140° and the compass shows 130°, turn to starboard until it reads 140°. To bring the number down, turn to port.

fig.note: Steer for the landmark, glance at the compass

blocks.p: A compass card swings with every wave and is tiring to stare at. Find something fixed that lies on your course, a headland or a tower, steer for it, and check the compass now and then.

A yacht answers the helm slowly. A beginner waits for the turn, adds more helm, and then swings past the course the other way. Give a small correction as soon as the bow starts to wander, bring the helm back, and wait for her to answer.

qa.q: What do the genoa tell-tales tell me when I'm steering close-hauled?
qa.a: If the windward **tell-tale** lifts you are too close to the wind, so bear away a little; if the leeward one lifts, luff up a little. Both streaming aft means you are on the wind.

blocks.p: No yacht sails straight into the wind: about 45° either side of it is the **no-go zone**. Close-hauled, you steer along its edge. To find the edge, head up slowly until the luff, the front edge of the genoa, starts to lift, then bear away a touch until the sail fills.

tiles.name: Close-hauled
tiles.note: along the edge of the no-go zone

tiles.name: Run
tiles.note: a turn towards the boom gybes her

blocks.p: **Tell-tales** are the strands of wool on each side of the genoa. Close-hauled with the sheets cleated, they tell the helm what to do.

On a **run** the wind is astern and the boom is right out on one side. If the stern swings through the wind, the boom slams across: an **accidental gybe**. It happens when the bow turns towards the side the boom is on. When a wave pushes the stern, correct at once and do not let the bow go that way.

sections.title: Warn, wait for the answer, then turn

qa.q: What does the helm call before tacking or gybing?
qa.a: First the warning, "Ready about!" or "Ready to gybe!"; then wait until every crew member answers "Ready!"; then call "Lee-oh!" or "Gybe-oh!" as you turn. No "Ready" from everyone, no turn.

blocks.p: The helm starts every tack and gybe, and the crew must know it is coming: sheets have to be handled, and the boom crosses the cockpit. Each turn has three steps.

fig.note: "Lee-oh!" as the bow turns into the wind

blocks.p: If one person has not answered, you wait. Someone still putting turns on a winch, or standing in the way of the boom, is not ready, and calling louder does not make them ready.

sections.title: No flow over the rudder, no steering

qa.q: Why won't the boat steer when I'm going very slowly in a marina?
qa.a: The **rudder** works only when water flows past it. Give a short burst ahead: the propeller throws water straight onto the rudder, and the bow turns before the boat gathers speed.

blocks.p: The rudder works only when water flows past it. Drifting with no way on, you can spin the wheel and nothing happens. So in a marina keep the speed **slow, but enough to steer**: no faster than you would be happy to hit something at, no slower than the rudder needs.

blocks.cap: The propeller sits just ahead of the rudder, so its wash reaches the blade at once.

list: Too slow and the bow will not answer: give a short burst ahead. The propeller throws water straight onto the rudder, and the bow turns before the boat gathers speed.
Going astern with a wheel, turn it the way you want the stern to go.
Putting the engine astern from a standstill, expect the stern to kick sideways first. This is **prop walk**. Which side depends on the boat: ask the skipper.

sections.title: Steady for the crew, clear for the next helm

qa.q: What should I tell the next person when I hand over the helm?
qa.a: What they cannot see at a glance: the **course**, the wind and how the sails are set, and any traffic to watch. Let go of the helm only when they say they have it.

blocks.p: Crew working at the mast or on the foredeck have no hand to spare. Hold a steady course, avoid sudden turns and heel, and warn them before any change.

When someone takes over, tell them what they cannot see at a glance: the **course**, the **wind** and how the sails are set, and any **traffic** to watch. Let go of the helm only when they say they have it.
